points.label: What the table shows
points.description: The learner describes the confusion matrix as a table comparing predicted classes against actual classes, where each cell counts examples with that (actual, predicted) combination — for binary classification: true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives.

points.label: The two error types are different
points.description: The learner explains that the matrix separates the two ways of being wrong — false positives (predicted positive, actually negative) and false negatives (predicted negative, actually positive) — and gives an example where the two errors have different real-world costs (e.g. spam filter vs disease screening).

points.label: Why accuracy alone misleads
points.description: The learner explains that a single accuracy number hides the error structure, especially with imbalanced classes: e.g. predicting 'negative' for everyone on a 99%-negative dataset scores 99% accuracy while the confusion matrix exposes that every positive was missed.

misconceptions.summary: High accuracy means the classifier is good, so there's no need to look at the individual cells.
misconceptions.correction: The learner explains that with imbalanced classes high accuracy can coexist with total failure on the minority class; the confusion matrix reveals this because the false-negative (or false-positive) cell stays large even when overall accuracy is high.

misconceptions.summary: A false positive and a false negative are equally bad — an error is an error.
misconceptions.correction: The learner clarifies that the costs of the two error types depend on the application: missing a cancer case (false negative) is far worse than a false alarm, while wrongly blocking a legitimate email (false positive) may be worse than letting one spam through — which is exactly why the matrix keeps them separate.

beginner: What do 'true positive' and 'false positive' actually mean? Which word refers to the prediction and which to reality?
Can you fill in a tiny confusion matrix for me with a concrete example, like a spam filter on 10 emails?
confident: My classifier is 99% accurate, so it's excellent — no need to dig into any matrix.
False positives and false negatives are interchangeable; any metric that lumps them together is fine.
skeptic: The matrix depends on the decision threshold I picked. Shift the threshold and every cell changes — so what does one matrix really tell me about the model?
The confusion matrix comes from one test set at one moment. If the class balance in production differs, aren't all these cell counts misleading?
